newsitem.title: USA: Moderation and investigation keywords of new Congress.
newsitem.headline: Moderation and investigation keywords of new Congress.

text.p: Republicans hope to steer safely down the middle when a new Congress convenes next year, ending talk of "revolution" that scared voters and presenting a scaled-down agenda emphasising budget and tax issues.

But sharp, partisan detours are likely as Republicans, who kept control of the House and Senate in Tuesday's balloting, escalate investigations into alleged White House scandals, including Democratic fundraising from foreign interests.
And while Republicans speak of moderate change, they have not abandoned their long-term commitment to dramatically cut the size of government and reduce regulation.
"This was a ratifying election," said Republican National Committee Chairman Haley Barbour. "(It) ratified the people's vote in 1994 when they rejected big government liberalism."

Republicans won a majority in the House and Senate in 1994 for the first time in 40 years. They fended off Democrats Tuesday to keep control -- the only time they have retained majorities in back-to-back Congresses in 68 years.

Republicans picked up at least two seats in the Senate, with voters electing more conservative lawmakers to replace retiring moderates. Republicans are still shy of the magic 60 votes needed to limit debate, giving Democrats vital leverage.
In the House, controversial Republican Newt Gingrich appears set to remain as speaker, but will preside over a diminished majority while facing ethics charges of his own.
Further, Democratic President Bill Clinton returns to the White House, with an incremental agenda focused on eduction and tax relief -- and an eye on compromise.

Those factors appear to set the stage for continuation of the pattern set last year when Republicans moved from revolution to moderation, compromising with Democrats and Clinton to pass health, welfare and minimum wage legislation.
"President Clinton was partially re-elected because he ran toward the Republicans. He ran to the centre," said Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican.
"If he's serious about those things and if he works in that direction, we're going to be able to do some good things for the American people," he said.

Lott said Republicans had not yet worked out a detailed agenda, but were committed to spending cuts needed to balance the budget, wanted to provide limited tax reductions while holding hearings on a possible overhaul of the entire income tax system and would try to reduce government regulation.
House aides said Republicans planned early votes on a balanced budget amendment and limits on lawmakers' terms.

Angry that Clinton co-opted many of their themes and accused them of slashing Medicare, Republicans may hang back initially and try to force Clinton to take the lead on difficult spending cuts and needed Medicare reforms.
"If (Republicans) revert to their old 'revolutionary' ways we will fight them. The next Congress must be about results, not revolutions," said Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle.
Republicans, who spent much of the past two years looking into Whitewater and alleged improprieties in the White House, have served notice they plan to step up their investigations.

At the top of the list are allegations that Democrats improperly solicited campaign contributions from foreign interests. Clinton managed to keep a lid on the controversy during the final weeks of the campaign, but will not be able to do so in coming months.
In a pre-emptive move, Clinton said in his victory speech that campaign finance reform would be a top item on his agenda and called for cooperation with Congress.
Lott said he expected early hearings, but denied Republicans were on a mission to get the president. "That is not our principal focus. Our job is to do the people's business," Lott declared.

Both Clinton and the Republicans learned painful lessons in the last four years. Clinton overreached with his sweeping health insurance plan that collapsed in 1994. Republicans promised a revolution, but it boomeranged when they were blamed for last winter's two government shutdowns.

As a result of those failures, the two sides made some efforts to work together. Gridlock is certainly possible, but in the immediate glow of re-election, lawmakers from both parties seem to believe the best way to protect their own political futures is to get things done.
